title: Arterial & neuropathic ulcers
summary: Ischaemic ulcers are punched-out, painful and distal, and must never be compressed. Neuropathic ulcers are painless, on plantar pressure points and surrounded by callus. Any diabetic foot ulcer needs urgent referral (NG19).

glance.think: Arterial: a punched-out, painful ulcer on the toes or lateral malleolus with a cold, pale, hairless foot. Neuropathic: a painless, deep ulcer under a metatarsal head ringed by callus.
glance.engine: Arterial: tissue ischaemia. Neuropathic: loss of protective sensation, with unnoticed repetitive trauma.
glance.backbone: Arterial: urgent vascular assessment and risk-factor treatment, with no compression. Neuropathic: offloading and the diabetic foot MDT.
glance.never_miss: Critical limb ischaemia, osteomyelitis (probe to bone), wet gangrene, and a ‘small’ plantar ulcer in diabetes.

head: Arterial (ischaemic) ulcer
Neuropathic ulcer (incl. diabetic foot)
rows: Loss of **protective sensation**, with or without deformity and ischaemia (‘neuro-ischaemic’)
Toes, heel, bony prominences, lateral malleolus, shin
**Plantar** metatarsal heads, heel, tips of toes
Deep, surrounded by **callus**; may reach bone
Often **severe**, worse on elevation and at night
Cold, pale or mottled, shiny, hairless, weak or absent pulses
Warm, with good pulses (unless neuro-ischaemic), dry skin, deformity

list: **Arterial:** atherosclerosis (or embolism) reduces flow, so poorly perfused sites become necrotic. Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, CKD and age.
**Neuropathic:** peripheral neuropathy (usually diabetes; also alcohol, B12 deficiency, leprosy) means repetitive trauma goes unnoticed. Deep ulcers can reach bone, with a risk of **osteomyelitis**.

features: See the comparison table under ‘What it is’. Arterial disease also causes **claudication**, rest pain (eased by hanging the leg out of bed) and dependent rubor. Neuropathic feet often have clawed toes, Charcot deformity and dry, fissured skin.

list: Examine pulses and measure **ABPI** (or TBPI in diabetes, where calcified vessels give falsely high ABPI).
Test sensation with a **10 g monofilament** and vibration.
**Probe to bone**, plus X-ray or MRI if osteomyelitis is suspected.
Urgent vascular assessment for critical limb ischaemia.

differentials: Venous ulcer, pressure ulcer (immobile patients, e.g. paraplegia), [pyoderma gangrenosum](condition:pyoderma-gangrenosum), vasculitis, and malignancy.

list: Urgent **vascular referral**, especially with rest pain, gangrene or critical ischaemia.
Risk factors: stop smoking, and give antiplatelet and statin therapy (per NICE CG147 and vascular advice). Optimise blood pressure and diabetes.
Analgesia, and wound care directed by tissue viability or vascular.
**Any diabetic foot ulcer:** refer urgently to the **multidisciplinary foot care service** or foot protection service (within 1 working day).
**Offloading**, glycaemic optimisation, and assessment for infection, which may need admission and IV antibiotics.
Diabetic foot infection: follow NICE NG19 and local antimicrobial guidance, and take deep tissue samples rather than surface swabs.

red_flags: **Critical limb ischaemia:** rest pain, gangrene, tissue loss, or a cold pulseless foot. **Same-day vascular.**
Diabetic foot with **spreading redness, fever, crepitus or wet necrosis**. **ED / same-day admission.**
Probe to bone, or suspected osteomyelitis or Charcot foot (hot, swollen foot in neuropathy).
**Never ignore a ‘small’ plantar ulcer in diabetes.**
pearls: **Any leg ulcer may be mixed.** Always assess the arterial supply before compression.
Teach **daily foot checks**, sensible footwear and podiatry follow-up, and never walk barefoot with neuropathy.
Painful ulcer worse on elevation suggests arterial. Painless ulcer under a callus suggests neuropathic.
